title: Knowledge Without Taxation? Experimental Evidence from a Tax Education Program (Jensen, Kumar & Poensgen), NBER Working Paper 36002, November 2026, DOI 10.3386/w36002

One ordinary request to the NBER PDF endpoint (system/files/working_papers/w36002/w36002.pdf) returned HTTP 403; not retried. verdict: NEW research/jensen-kumar-poensgen-tax-education-ghana (page name suggestion). Precedent: research/tourek-drc-progressive-property-tax. Also ENRICH three existing pages with a short cross-link (see existing_wiki_coverage). Fit caveat: this is a property-tax compliance RCT, not a land-tax study; the page must say it tests no land value tax and that the Ghana base is building value (per King 2026 on the wiki) and the paper is silent on land.
claim_grade: B (empirical; NBER working paper, not peer reviewed; a single-municipality RCT, small cluster count) with Tier 1 source standing (NBER working-paper series; Jensen is at Harvard Kennedy School and an NBER affiliate; Kumar and Poensgen at Harvard; fieldwork partner IGC/Boston University co-investigators in the registry). Registry entry is A-claim for design facts only. Author-interpretive statements (e.g. 'knowledge is a double-edged sword', mechanism readings) are C/D and must be attributed to the authors. Not in sources/audit/people-tiers.json (grep found no Jensen/Poensgen entry): judged by rubric as recognised scholars.

content_summary.setting_and_sample: Ablekuma Central, an urban district (municipality) in Greater Accra, Ghana. Fieldwork Aug-Nov 2024 (intervention 9 Sep-20 Oct 2024 per registry). 24 frontline tax officials (the entire set available), 48 collection units (24 pairs, one per wave; ~60 properties per unit; units halved vs normal six-week campaign), baseline survey of 1,193 property owners (target 25 per unit), endline N=1,108 (7% attrition, balanced), midline phone survey 319 of 595 wave-2 households. Residential or mixed-use properties only; purely commercial excluded; wealthiest and poorest units excluded (pp.15, 20-21). Registry planned ~1,250 households. Context: property-tax compliance 5-15% (<15% in this district; control-group endline payment rate 12%; control bill receipt 31%) (pp.1, 7-8). Baseline knowledge: 92% of households could not name any property characteristic determining liability; 93% could not name the institution responsible for valuation (p.9).
content_summary.design_correction: The scanner's 'two treatment arms (owners; officials)' is incomplete. Design is a control group plus three treatment groups, randomised at collection-unit-pair level with households randomised 50/50 within treated units: CG (nobody educated); TG1 (about half of surveyed owners educated, officials not); TG2 (TG1 plus officials told which two areas have a high density of educated owners); TG3 (TG2 plus officials receive the same workshop). Households are 'TG-treated' or 'TG-untreated' (13 untreated, 12 treated per unit). Intervention: concise preview at end of baseline survey, a workshop by a private-sector tax lawyer (content built with Accra's Institute of Local Government Studies; rights and responsibilities in equal weight; Local Governance Act), and a hotline (only workshop-logistics calls recorded). Workshop attendance among TG-treated was 23% (pp.2-3, 12-16, 'one in four' p.17). The registry additionally describes a second 'Experiment 1' (four taxpayer-collector pairings); the paper text read does not report it as a separate experiment: do not cite it.
headline_estimates: Abstract (verbatim, NBER and paper cover): 'The intervention raises tax knowledge, which spreads through social networks to untreated neighbors, but does not increase tax payments.'

Knowledge, TG-treated (Table 1, p.40): endline declarative index +0.16 SD (se 0.07, p<0.05), driven by process index +0.40 (se 0.13, p<0.01) and rights +0.18 (se 0.08); practical 'taxpayer action' index +0.54 (se 0.13, p<0.01); self-perceived knowledge +0.18 (se 0.05). Midline (Panel A): declarative index +0.20 (se 0.08, p<0.05), process +0.29 (se 0.10). Officials in TG3 (Panel C, n=21): rights +1.46 SD (se 0.38), formula +0.78 (se 0.36), index +0.38 (se 0.26, n.s.).

Spillover to untreated households (Table 1 Panel B col.7, p.40): TG-untreated practical-knowledge index +0.32 SD (se 0.12, p<0.01); declarative index +0.01 (n.s.), self-perceived +0.11 (se 0.06, p<0.1). Conversations (Table 2, p.41): TG-untreated +11 pp likelier to speak to anyone about property tax (se 0.04; CG mean 4%, a 275% rise), TG-treated +16 pp. Social multiplier 1.6 for practical knowledge, 1.7 for conversations, identified with Borusyak-Hull re-centred exposure (pp.24-26, Figure 1, Table A.9); the authors call these lower bounds.

Null on tax outcomes (Table 3, p.41; N=1,108, self-reported endline): any payment TG-untreated -0.02 (se 0.04), TG-treated +0.01 (se 0.04), CG mean 0.12; official visit +0.02/+0.03 (CG 0.13); received bill +0.01/-0.01 (CG 0.31); payment amount -17.39 (se 24.38) / -8.01 (se 22.51) against CG mean 72.66 (currency not stated in the extract; presumably GH cedi, check). Confirmed by administrative daily reports (Table 4: only significant item is fewer registrations in TG2, -7.68) and by tablet GPS records (Table 5): no effect on visits or time with owners, no targeting of highlighted 'educated' areas (pp.27-28). Payment is self-reported; the 12% control rate is close to observed rates in Ghana per the authors (p.27).

Mechanisms (Tables 6-8, pp.31-36, 43-44): (a) interactions: TG households report higher self-assessment and engagement in dealings with officials (Table 6 col.1, strongly positive, nearly as large for untreated as treated) but do not rate officials better; the authors read this as 'no movement towards more co-productive, collaborative relationships'; TG3 officials show qualitatively similar but smaller effects (pp.4, 31-33). (b) tax planning: knowledge of bill reduction, revaluation and instalment requests rises, no uptake (Table 7, p.34-35); reasons for non-use include judging the grounds not applicable or that the assembly will not grant them (Table A.19). (c) tax morale: no effect on any of five components (Table 8 cols.1-5, p.44; e.g. satisfaction/competence -0.028 (se 0.041) treated). (d) enforcement beliefs (Table 8 col.6, p.44): reported % of residential owners who pay: TG-untreated -6.010 (se 2.489, p<0.05), TG-treated -4.394 (se 2.611, p<0.1) vs CG mean 56.178, against a true ~12%; authors read CG as over-estimating enforcement and treated households as updating correctly (p.36). Authors' conclusion: 'Education thus stimulates agency without fostering trust in or outright acceptance of the taxation process' (p.4).
content_summary.limits_stated_by_authors: Light-touch, purely informational, government-neutral content (no references to assembly performance), so external validity to government-led campaigns is limited; null may reflect insufficient intensity; 24 officials only; shifts in enforcement beliefs may be too small to move payment; midline and some outcomes use random sub-samples (pp.13, 23).
content_summary.tax_base_valuation: Ghana's property rate base: the paper describes only that the local government 'sets the tax rates levied on the property valuations (distinguished by property use and geographic area)' (Section 2.1, p.7), that officially valued properties are those valued by the Ghana Lands Commission plus municipality-registered ones (fn.18, p.15), and that owners can request revaluation or a bill reduction. It does NOT say whether land or buildings is valued, does not mention land value, site value, capital or rental value, and studies no land-based tax. Land does not enter the paper except through the Lands Commission reference. The building-value fact for the wiki rests on the King (2026) page, not this paper. Revaluation requests are the only valuation-linked margin tested (Table 7).
content_summary.lvt_relevance: Indirect. Evidence on whether informing taxpayers raises compliance of a local recurrent property tax in a low-capacity setting; null effect plus lowered enforcement beliefs; adds to the state-capacity literature already on the wiki (Bergeron-Tourek-Weigel; Tourek et al.). Georgist angle only by inference (administrative preconditions for any recurrent land or property tax); must be labelled analysis, not the authors' claim. The authors cite Brockmeyer et al. 2021, Bergeron-Tourek-Weigel 2024 and Henn et al. 2026 (DRC consultants) as related work (p.6).

wrong_or_incomplete: 'Two treatment arms' understates the design: CG + TG1/TG2/TG3, household-level randomisation inside units
'Frontline officials' treated only in TG3, one arm of three; TG2 gives officials only a map of educated areas
'Payments do not move' rests on self-reported endline data (corroborated for visits/registrations by admin and GPS data, not for payments)
Scanner calls it 'citable primary working paper complementing the JIE King paper': true but King is qualitative on land/tax authority divergence; this paper has no land content
'Awareness of legal avoidance' is knowledge of three lawful requests (bill reduction, revaluation, instalments), not tax avoidance or evasion; take-up was null

title: Pakistan: New World Bank Program to Strengthen Municipal Revenues and Services in Sindh (World Bank press release, 30 Oct 2026); program P517498, Sindh Property Revenues Enhancement Program (Sindh PREP)
what_was_fetched: Press release in full (HTTP 200; item2-press-release.txt). Its 'Project Documents' link gives P517498 and the Concept Program Information Document (PID, 14 Jul 2026, 4 pp.; dl2/P517498.pdf, item2-wb-doc-P517498.txt). projects.worldbank.org project-detail page fetched once (HTTP 200, JS shell, item2-projectpage.html, no usable text). verdict: REJECT as a standalone page (press release is not a research object). ENRICH places/pakistan.md with a short 'Sindh PREP' paragraph sourced to the Program Paper (Tier 1 primary), with the press release only as the announcement; optionally an events/ entry if the wiki carries an events page for Board approvals. Also correct the devolution date on pakistan.md (see uncertainties).
claim_grade: A for programme facts (approval, amounts, structure, indicators) as the Bank's own statements; B for the Karachi collection and comparison figures (Bank analysis from 'City Financial Statistics latest data accessible and Valuation Rolls', not independently sourced); C for projections (US$85m, US$172m at 70% compliance, 70% reinvestment as intended design). Tier 1 institutional (World Bank). The Program Paper is a Bank staff appraisal and advocacy-adjacent for its own operation: attribute as 'the Bank's appraisal states'.

content_summary.press_release: Board approved US$150 million 30 Oct 2026; Sindh PREP to improve UIPT collection and municipal service delivery. Karachi 'collects only approximately US$8.5 million annually in property tax while cities of similar size collect 82 to 350 times more'; target US$85 million annually 'raising compliance from 20 to 50 percent'; UIPT MIS for billing, payment processing, grievance redress; IFMIS rollout; 'About 70 percent of collected UIPT revenues will be reinvested' in participating councils; 25 Karachi local councils, 'primary beneficiaries are the 3.58 million people living in these councils'; annual performance assessments by an Independent Verification Agent determine each council's awards; IPF component US$40 million for property surveys and UIPT administration in 20 councils in other urban centres, 'indirect benefit to approximately 4.5 million people'. Quote: local councils depend on provincial transfers for 'more than 95 percent of their revenues' (Country Director Bolormaa Amgaabazar).
program_paper_figures: Karachi US$8.5m vs cities 'of similar population size (between 20-24 million)' collecting 82 to 350 times more: Mumbai US$699m, Mexico City US$1.2bn, Sao Paulo US$3bn; also smaller cities Windhoek US$40m, Nairobi US$27.5m, Harare US$96m, Johannesburg US$940m (para 13, p.3; fn 19: 'City Financial Statistics latest data accessible and Valuation Rolls'). Wording: 'Karachi collects a paltry US$8.5 million'.

US$85m target: 'Raising compliance from 20 to 50 percent could increase Karachi's UIPT revenue by 10 times from US$8.5 million to US$85 million, and to US$172 million at 70 percent compliance' (para 13, p.3); PDO Indicator 1 'Annual UIPT revenue increased from approximately US$8.5 million to US$85 million' (para 19, p.5). Fn 20: calculated after discounting 44.3% of properties as non-taxable (1,949,200) per the old database; average revenue per property US$71.25 a year.

Compliance baseline inconsistency: the results framework (Annex, p.27) lists 'UIPT compliance rate (Percentage)' baseline 12, end target 50, measured as challans paid / challans generated in the MIS in the 25 Karachi councils, with a footnote that the baseline is a proxy 'due to data gaps'; delivery rate of challans baseline 12, target 70. The body text and press release say 20. Report both and say which is which.

70% reinvestment: 'In addition, 70 percent of collected UIPT revenues will be reinvested in infrastructure and services that benefit local communities' (para 18, p.5); counted as indirect counterpart funding: 'roughly US$60 million annually, or US$300 million over the Program period' (para 31, p.10). It is a design commitment of the Program, not an observed rule.

25 councils: Karachi's 25 LCs established in 2023 (previously seven district councils, restructured 2021) (para 8, p.2). The 3.58 million is NOT the councils' population: fn 23 (p.9) says it assumes 20% of the population are direct beneficiaries of financed investments; total population in the 25 councils is 17.8 million (para 26 says 17.9 million, 8.6 million women; fn 23 says 17.8). Correct the scanner's '25 Karachi councils (3.58 million residents)'.

Results-based structure: PforR credit; three DLIs funded US$110m (RA1 UIPT collection, compliance and administration US$65m; RA2 revenue and expenditure management, IFMIS, US$15m; RA3 municipal service delivery US$30m) (Table, p.7; DLI table p.10-11); award allocations by each council's Annual Performance Assessment score weighted by its OZT share (Octroi and Zila Tax share); IVA conducts the APA annually each July (Table 4, p.8; para 33-34, p.11; para 54, p.14); disbursement on IVA verification, with a Bank quality-assurance review that prevails if findings differ. Average annual award per council about US$1.1m (range US$0.4-2m); total over the period US$1.3m (smallest) to US$7.2m (largest) (para 24, p.8).

IPF component US$40m: technical assistance, programme management (US$6m), Karachi (US$10m) and 'UIPT and Modernization of UIPT and Land Administration across 20 LCs outside of Karachi' (US$24m) (para 25 and fn 22, p.9); about 60% of the IPF is outside Karachi; GIS door-to-door surveys with third-party validation for 'more than 2 million properties'; BoR support for 'digitizing and updating land records, and conducting city surveys'. Outside Karachi, five secondary cities (11m population) have only 400,000 of an estimated 2.1m properties in the UIPT cadaster; surveys could 'expand the property tax base more than fivefold' (para 15, p.3-4). Indirect beneficiaries about 4.5 million (the document gives 4.6 million total population in the other councils, 48% women) (para 27, fn 24, p.9).

UIPT MIS: GIS-based, built under CLICK (Competitive and Livable City of Karachi, P161402), eight core functions: property mapping and geo-referencing; field survey and data collection; property database management; assessment and valuation; property management; tax management; grievance redress; citizen mobile app for payments (para 11 and fn 17, p.3). CLICK raised Karachi's UIPT base from 976,000 to 4.5 million properties via the first survey in nearly 25 years (last 2001).

Financing: IDA Scale-Up Window credit of US$150m (para 30, p.10); total operation cost US$180.4m incl. counterpart US$30.4m (Table 6, p.10). The earlier concept PID (Jul 2026) shows IBRD financing, total programme US$110m and PDO 'in 45 local councils'; the approved paper says IDA. Programme period FY2026/27-FY2030/31 (Table 4, p.8).
content_summary.devolution_note: The wiki's pakistan.md says collection 'devolved to local councils from September 2024 (p.14)' of Lucas-Mas & Touqeer. The Program Paper (para 7, p.2) gives a different chronology: Chief Minister's notification devolving UIPT collection to councils in September 2021; Excise and Taxation Department transferred records, registries and collection functions the following year; 'LCs began collecting UIPT in FY 2024/25' (July 2024-June 2025); Sindh described as the first province to devolve UIPT to councils; budget-speech origin FY2017/18. So 'September 2024' is not supported by this primary; likely the two sources describe different steps or the earlier report is imprecise. Do not repeat the lead's 'September 2024' without checking the 44905 report p.14; at minimum add the Bank's own chronology.
content_summary.valuation_basis: The Program Paper does not state whether UIPT in Sindh is levied on annual rental value or capital value, and does not mention land value, site value or a land-only tax. Valuation appears only as: the UIPT MIS has an 'assessment and valuation' function (fn 17); the Board of Revenue 'is responsible for updating valuation tables' (para 41, p.12); and para 13 (p.3) states that raising 'the tax rate and property values' is 'outside the scope of PREP', with the programme focused on base (done under CLICK) and compliance. Para 69 (p.17) cites studies that Karachi could raise revenue 'through revaluation, tax-base expansion, exemption rationalization, and stronger collection without raising tax rates' (fn 29: World Bank 2024, Realizing the Potential of Pakistan's Secondary Cities; World Bank 2022, The Property Taxation Scenario in Pakistan). Land enters only as land records and cadastre: results area on 'digitize and update land and property records' with BoR, a cadastral index rising from 0.626 to 0.899 in divisional headquarters outside Karachi (p.20), and 'modernization of UIPT and land administration' (IPF). Hence the programme is compliance and base-expansion, consistent with the wiki's statement that the Pakistan story is administration, not a land value tax, and silent on the rental-to-capital-value shift.
